tagline: Gravel forest roads follow a trout river through reforested mountain country
intro: Williams River Road follows a boulder-strewn riverbed between densely forested hills on narrow gravel Forest Roads 86 and 216. West Virginia’s Byways and Backways guide gives the route 28 miles and an hour’s driving time. Designated in August 1998, the backway offers fishing, camping and access to trails in the Cranberry Wilderness and Tea Creek Backcountry. The river averages 40 feet across, with pools and underwater cover. The Forest Service describes its watershed as moderately stable, so the water is slow to become turbid.

The forest along much of the river grew back after heavy logging in the early twentieth century. Coal mining continued along the lower river into the 1970s. Cranberry Wilderness was established in 1983, and a 2009 addition protected tributaries of both the Williams and Cranberry rivers.

From the Cowen end, follow the lower river upstream toward Dyer, on County Route 46. Forest Road 86 closely follows the Williams, with access farther along the corridor to wilderness trails and Tea Creek campground. The backway reaches toward the river’s headwaters in Pocahontas County; the river itself begins on Black Mountain. The Highland Scenic Highway provides access to the middle section, while Secondary Route 17 off Route 219 reaches the upper end.

moments.title: Dyer
moments.text: Dyer began as Haynes, a village on the Williams River that received a post office in 1893. George M. Dyer became its postmaster that year and held the job until 1923. In 1911 the village took his name. The post office closed in 1938, and mail went to Cowen instead. Dyer remains a community on the river and County Route 46, east-southeast of Cowen.

moments.title: Cranberry Wilderness
moments.text: At Three Forks, the Williams River leaves Cranberry Wilderness at its lowest elevation, 2,400 feet. The protected area rises into the Yew Mountains and is also a designated black bear sanctuary. Established in 1983, it expanded in 2009 into land between the Williams and Cranberry rivers. That addition protects tributaries of both rivers and has trails connected to the original wilderness. The backway provides access to many miles of wilderness hiking trails. The mountains drain in two directions here: the Williams and Cranberry both feed the Gauley, while land just east of the wilderness drains toward the Greenbrier.

moments.title: Tea Creek
moments.text: Tea Creek was named for water stained brown like tea. Its campground is one of two named river campgrounds in the state’s backways guide, alongside Day Run. Other primitive campsites line the corridor, and the road gives access to trails in the Tea Creek Backcountry.

practical: Dyer: The backway’s narrow forest roads are drivable from spring through fall and are not maintained through winter. RVs should proceed with caution. (checked 2026-10-11)
